docs.text: G-CODES FOR DELTA X S V5 ¶ G0, G1 - Linear Movement ¶ Descriptions ¶ The G0 and G1 commands add a linear MOVE to the queue to be performed after all previous moves are completed. Set F (feed rate), A (acceleration), J (jerk), S (start velocity), and E (end velocity) once. Subsequent movement commands use these settings until changed; motion parameters omitted from a command keep their current settings. Usage ¶ G1 [X<pos>] [Y<pos>] [Z<pos>] [W<angle>] [U<angle>] [V<angle>] [F<val>] [A<val>] [J<val>] [S<val>] [E<val>] Parameters ¶ Parameter Description X[pos] (mm) A coordinate on the X-axis. Y[pos] (mm) A coordinate on the Y-axis. Z[pos] (mm) A coordinate on the Z-axis. W[angle] (unit) Axis 4 position. U[angle] (unit) Axis 5 position. V[angle] (unit) Axis 6 position. F[val] (mm/s) The maximum movement rate of the move between the start and endpoint. The feedrate set here applies to subsequent moves that omit this parameter. A[val] (mm/s2) Acceleration of the motion. J[val] (mm/s3) Jerk of the motion. S[val] (mm/s) Begin velocity. E[val] (mm/s) Finish velocity. For W/U/V, a unit is a degree for a rotary axis or a millimeter for a linear axis, according to its steps-per-unit configuration. Example ¶ G01 F1500 A15000 J550000 S100 E100 ; Set the feed rate to 1500 mm/s, acceleration to 15000 mm/s², jerk to 550000 mm/s³, start velocity to 100 mm/s, and end velocity to 100 mm/s. G01 X0 Y0 Z-750 ; Move to the absolute position (X0, Y0, Z-750). G01 X50 ; Move to X = 50 mm. G01 W90 ; Rotate to 90° on the 4-axis G2, G3 - Controlled Arc Movement ¶ Descriptions ¶ G2 adds a clockwise arc move to the planner; G3 adds a counter-clockwise arc. The arc runs in the XY plane from the current position to the specified X/Y endpoint, keeping Z unchanged. I and J locate the center relative to the arc’s starting point. Usage ¶ G02 I<offset> J<offset> [X<pos>] [Y<pos>] [W<angle>] [U<angle>] [V<angle>] [F<val>] [A<val>] [S<val>] [E<val>] Use G03 for a counter-clockwise arc. Always include both I and J , even when one offset is zero. In these commands, J is the Y center offset; the previously configured jerk remains in use. Parameters ¶ Parameter Description I[offset] (mm) Required X offset from the starting point to the arc center. J[offset] (mm) Required Y offset from the starting point to the arc center. X[pos] (mm) A coordinate on the X-axis. Y[pos] (mm) A coordinate on the Y-axis. W[angle] , U[angle] , V[angle] :(unit) Axis 4, 5, and 6 positions, using the configured units for each axis. F[val] (mm/s) The maximum movement rate of the move between the start and endpoint. The feedrate set here applies to subsequent moves that omit this parameter. A[val] (mm/s2) Acceleration of the motion. S[val] (mm/s) Begin velocity. E[val] (mm/s) Finish velocity. Example ¶ G28 ; Home all axes. G90 ; Use absolute positioning. G01 X50 Y0 Z-750 F200 ; Move to the arc start at (X50, Y0, Z-750). G02 X0 Y-50 I-50 J0 F200 ; Clockwise 90° arc around (X0, Y0), radius 50 mm. G03 X50 Y0 I0 J50 F200 ; Counter-clockwise 90° arc back to (X50, Y0). Both arcs keep Z at -750 mm. The X/Y endpoints are absolute positions; I/J are offsets from each arc’s starting point to the center at (X0, Y0). G4 - Dwell/Delay ¶ Descriptions ¶ Pause the robot for a period of time. Usage ¶ G4 P<value> Parameters ¶ Parameter Description P[value] delay in milliseconds. Example ¶ G01 X0 Y0 Z-750 F1500 A15000 J550000 S100 E100 G4 P500 ;delay 500ms G01 X50 G6 - Theta angle control ¶ Descriptions ¶ Specify the target Theta 1, 2, and 3 angles instead of Cartesian endpoint coordinates. Axis 6 is selected with R in this command. Usage ¶ G6 [X<angle>] [Y<angle>] [Z<angle>] [W<pos>] [U<pos>] [R<pos>] [F<val>] [A<val>] [J<val>] [S<val>] [E<val>] Parameters ¶ Parameter Description X[angle] (degree) The value of the Theta 1 angle. Y[angle] (degree) The value of the Theta 2 angle. Z[angle] (degree) The value of the Theta 3 angle. W[pos] (unit) Axis 4 position. U[pos] (unit) Axis 5 position. R[pos] (unit) Axis 6 position. F[val] (mm/s) Cartesian feed rate. A[val] (mm/s²) Cartesian acceleration. J[val] (mm/s³) Cartesian jerk. S[val] (mm/s) Start velocity. E[val] (mm/s) End velocity. W/U/R use the configured units for their axes: degrees for rotary axes or millimeters for linear axes. Omitted F/A/J/S/E values keep their current motion settings, which also apply to subsequent moves until changed. Example ¶ G90 ; Use absolute positioning. G6 X20 Y0 Z0 F200 ; Move to Theta 1 = 20°, Theta 2 = 0°, Theta 3 = 0° at 200 mm/s. G28 - Homing ¶ Descriptions ¶ Auto-home all axes, moving them towards their endstops until triggered. Usage ¶ G28 G90 - Absolute Movement Mode ¶ Descriptions ¶ In absolute mode, all coordinates given in G-code are interpreted as positions in the logical coordinate space. Usage ¶ G90 G91 - Relative Movement Mode ¶ Descriptions ¶ Set relative position mode. In this mode, all coordinates are interpreted as relative to the last position. Usage ¶ G91 G93 - Get Current Position ¶ Descriptions ¶ Read the current Cartesian position and the positions of enabled auxiliary axes. Usage ¶ G93 Feedback ¶ The response begins with <xpos>,<ypos>,<zpos> in millimeters. Positions of enabled W, U, and V axes follow in that order, using each axis’s configured units. Disabled axes are omitted. Values have two decimal places. Positive values have no leading + sign or zero padding. Example ¶ G93 ; Read the current position. Example response with auxiliary axes disabled: 0.00,0.00,-750.00 Example response with only axis W enabled, at 90°: 0.00,0.00,-750.00,90.00 M03, M04 - Set Digital Output / PWM ¶ Descriptions ¶ Set digital output states or PWM values. M03 uses 8-bit PWM values; M04 uses 16-bit PWM values. Both commands can set digital outputs with D . Usage ¶ M03 D<pin> W<state> M04 D<pin> W<state> M03 P<pin> W<value> M04 P<pin> W<value> Parameters ¶ Parameter Values and function D<pin> Digital output index: 0 – 7 . Use W1 to turn it on or W0 to turn it off. P<pin> PWM output index: 0 – 7 . W<value> with M03 P... 8-bit PWM value: 0 – 255 . W<value> with M04 P... 16-bit PWM value: 0 – 65535 . Always include W , including for digital outputs. Several outputs can be selected on one line, such as M03 D0 D1 W1 . D and P select digital or PWM control of the output with that index. Example ¶ M03 D0 W1 ; Turn on digital output D0. M03 D1 D2 W1 ; Turn on digital outputs D1 and D2. M03 P3 W128 ; Set PWM output P3 to 128 on the 8-bit scale (0–255). M04 P4 W32768 ; Set PWM output P4 to 32768 on the 16-bit scale (0–65535). M03 D0 W0 ; Turn off digital output D0. Each command returns Ok . M05 - Turn Off Digital Output / PWM ¶ Descriptions ¶ Turn off selected digital outputs or set selected PWM outputs to zero. Usage ¶ M05 D<pin> M05 P<pin> Parameters ¶ Parameter Values and function D<pin> Digital output index: 0 – 7 . Set the selected output to OFF. P<pin> PWM output index: 0 – 7 . Set the selected PWM value to zero. Several outputs can be selected on one line. Specify at least one D or P output; a bare M05 does not select all outputs. Example ¶ M03 D0 W1 ; Turn on digital output D0. M05 D0 ; Turn off digital output D0. M03 P1 W128 ; Set PWM output P1 to 128 on the 8-bit scale. M05 P1 ; Set PWM output P1 to zero. M05 D2 D3 P4 ; Turn off D2 and D3, and set PWM output P4 to zero. Each command returns Ok . M07 - Read Input Signals. ¶ Descriptions ¶ Read the current state of selected digital inputs or the raw ADC values of selected analog inputs. Several digital and analog channels can be requested on one line. Usage ¶ M07 I<pin> M07 A<pin> M07 I<digital_pin> A<analog_pin> Parameters ¶ Parameter Values and function I<pin> Digital input index: 0 – 5 . A<pin> Analog input index: 0 or 1 . Feedback ¶ Response Meaning I<pin> V<value> Digital input state: 0 or 1 . A<pin> V<value> Raw 12-bit ADC value: 0 – 4095 . One response is returned per selected input when the I/O board replies. Specify at least one input from the ranges above. Example ¶ M07 I0 I3 A1 ; Read digital inputs I0 and I3, and analog input A1. Example responses; values depend on the connected signals: I0 V1 I3 V0 A1 V2478 M08 - Read Input Signals Automatically. ¶ Descriptions ¶ Configure automatic input reports. Digital inputs report state changes; analog inputs report sampled values at the requested interval. Usage ¶ M08 I<pin> [B<enable>] [P<port>] M08 A<pin> [C<period_us>] [P<port>] Parameters ¶ Parameter Values and function I<pin> Digital input index: 0 – 5 . Several inputs can be selected on one line. B<enable> Digital reports: 1 enables reporting; 0 disables it. Default: 1 when omitted. A<pin> Analog input index: 0 or 1 . Both channels can be selected on one line. C<period_us> Requested analog report period in microseconds. Default: 500000 (500 ms) when omitted. The I/O-board firmware determines the supported minimum period and the value used to disable analog reports. P<port> Report destination: 0 = USB0, 1 = RS232, 2 = RS485, 3 = USB1. The startup report destination is USB0. Open the selected serial port before requesting reports on it. RS485 ( P2 ) requires full-duplex mode; half-duplex mode returns Unknown: This function cannot be used on RS485! . Ethernet ( P4 ) is not accepted by M08 . Digital inputs assigned to an enabled emergency stop are used for E-stop monitoring instead of ordinary automatic digital reports. Feedback ¶ Each configuration command returns Ok . Reports then arrive as: Response Meaning I<pin> V<value> Digital input state: 0 or 1 . A<pin> V<value> Raw 12-bit ADC value: 0 – 4095 . Example ¶ M08 I3 B1 P0 ; Report changes on digital input I3 through USB0. M08 A1 C500000 P0 ; Request analog input A1 reports every 500 ms through USB0. Example automatic reports; values depend on the connected signals: I3 V0 A1 V2478 To stop automatic reports for digital input I3: M08 I3 B0 ; Disable automatic reports for digital input I3. M40 - Open RS232 port. ¶ Descriptions ¶ Enable/Disable RS232 port and set baudrate. Usage ¶ M40 A<x> [B<y>] Parameters ¶ M40 A[x] B[y] A[x] : Open/Close RS232 port x = 1 : Open Port x = 0 : Close port B[y] : baud rate. Example ¶ M40 A1 B115200 ;Open RS232 port and set baudrate at 115200 M41 - Open RS485 port ¶ Descriptions ¶ Enable/Disable RS485 port and set baudrate. Usage ¶ M41 A<x> [B<y>] Parameters ¶ M41 A[x] B[y] A[x] : Open/Close RS485 port x = 1 : Open Port x = 0 : Close Port B[y] : baud rate. Note: When control Delta X S via RS485, after each time sending a G-code command to the robot, you must wait for a response from the robot before sending the next G-code command. Otherwise, the communication will not be successful. Example ¶ M41 A1 B115200 ;Open RS485 port and set baudrate at 115200 M42 - Open USB1 port. ¶ Descriptions ¶ Enable/Disable USB1 port and set baudrate. Usage ¶ M42 A<x> [B<y>] Parameters ¶ M42 A[x] B[y] A[x] : Open/Close USB1 port x = 1 : Open Port x = 0 : Close Port B[y] : baud rate. Example ¶ M42 A1 B115200 ; Enable USB1 and set the baud rate to 115200. M49 - Get Ports Config ¶ Descriptions ¶ Read the enabled state and configured baud rate of USB0, RS232, RS485, and USB1. The response labels USB0 as USB . Usage ¶ M49 Example ¶ M49 Example response; enabled states and baud rates depend on the current configuration: USB:1 BAUD:115200 RS232:0 BAUD:115200 RS485:1 BAUD:115200 USB1:1 BAUD:115200 M50 - Enable RJ45 ¶ Descriptions ¶ This command can be used to enable or disable RJ45 port. Usage ¶ M50 A<x> Parameter ¶ A[x] x = 1 : enable RJ45 x = 0 : disable RJ45 Example ¶ M50 A1 ; enable RJ45 M51 - Set Ethernet Port ¶ Descriptions ¶ Set ethernet port number Usage ¶ M51 B<x> Parameter ¶ Parameter Description B[x] port number Example ¶ M51 B8080 ; set ethernet port M52 - Set MAC Device ¶ Descriptions ¶ Set the robot’s MAC address and save it to EEPROM. Usage ¶ Provide all six bytes in A:B:C:D:E:F order, using decimal integers from 0 to 255. M52 A<x> B<y> C<z> D<t> E<u> F<v> Parameter ¶ Parameter Description A[x] number B[y] number C[z] number D[t] number E[u] number F[v] number Example ¶ M52 A2 B23 C34 D45 E56 F67 ; Set MAC address 02:17:22:2D:38:43 (hex). Response: Ok M53 - Set Ethernet IP ¶ Descriptions ¶ Set the robot’s Ethernet IP address and save it to EEPROM. A/B/C/D are the four address octets, each a decimal integer from 0 to 255; all four are required. Usage ¶ M53 A<x> B<y> C<z> D<t> Parameter ¶ Parameter Description A[x] number B[y] number C[z] number D[t] number Example ¶ M53 A192 B168 C1 D98 ; Set the robot IP address to 192.168.1.98. Response: Ok M54 - Set Ethernet DNS ¶ Descriptions ¶ Set the Ethernet DNS server address and save it to EEPROM. A/B/C/D are the four address octets, each a decimal integer from 0 to 255; all four are required. Usage ¶ M54 A<x> B<y> C<z> D<t> Parameter ¶ Parameter Description A[x] number B[y] number C[z] number D[t] number Example ¶ M54 A192 B168 C1 D1 ; Set the DNS server to 192.168.1.1. Response: Ok M55 - Set Ethernet Gateway ¶ Descriptions ¶ Set the Ethernet gateway address and save it to EEPROM. A/B/C/D are the four address octets, each a decimal integer from 0 to 255; all four are required. Usage ¶ M55 A<x> B<y> C<z> D<t> Parameter ¶ Parameter Description A[x] number B[y] number C[z] number D[t] number Example ¶ M55 A192 B168 C1 D1 ; Set the gateway to 192.168.1.1. M56 - Set Ethernet Subnet ¶ Descriptions ¶ Set the Ethernet subnet mask and save it to EEPROM. A/B/C/D are the four mask octets, each a decimal integer from 0 to 255; all four are required. Usage ¶ M56 A<x> B<y> C<z> D<t> Parameter ¶ Parameter Description A[x] number B[y] number C[z] number D[t] number Example ¶ M56 A255 B255 C255 D0 ; Set the subnet mask to 255.255.255.0. M57 - Get Robot IP ¶ Descriptions ¶ Read the robot’s configured Ethernet IP address. Usage ¶ M57 Example ¶ M57 Example response after setting the IP address to 192.168.1.98: IP:192.168.1.98 M60 - Set Axis 4 Parameters ¶ Descriptions ¶ Configure axis 4 and save its configuration to EEPROM. Units are degrees for a rotary axis or millimeters for a linear axis, according to the steps-per-unit setting. Usage ¶ M60 [D<val>] [E<val>] [I<val>] [S<val>] [R<val>] [U<val>] [P<val>] [Q<val>] [H<val>] [A<val>] [J<val>] [F<val>] Parameter ¶ D[val] : enable axis 4 val = 1 : enable axis 4 val = 0 : disable axis 4 E[val] : enable endstop val = 1 : enable axis 4 endstop val = 0 : disable axis 4 endstop I[val] : set invert endstop logic level val = 1 : axis 4 endstop invert val = 0 : axis 4 endstop non-invert S[val] : (unit/s) homing speed R[val] : (unit) distance to back away from the endstop during homing U[val] : (step/unit) set step/unit parameter P[val] : (unit) set max position Q[val] : (unit) set min position H[val] : (unit) set home position A[val] : (unit/s²) maximum acceleration J[val] : (unit/s³) maximum jerk F[val] : (unit/s) maximum velocity Example ¶ M60 D1 E1 I0 S15 R5 U8.333 P178 Q0 H45 A4000 J900000 F2000 In this example, R5 sets a 5-unit homing back-off distance. Use configuration values appropriate for the connected axis. M61 - Set Axis 5 Parameters ¶ Descriptions ¶ Configure axis 5 and save its configuration to EEPROM. Units are degrees for a rotary axis or millimeters for a linear axis, according to the steps-per-unit setting. Usage ¶ M61 [D<val>] [E<val>] [I<val>] [S<val>] [R<val>] [U<val>] [P<val>] [Q<val>] [H<val>] [A<val>] [J<val>] [F<val>] Parameter ¶ D[val] : enable axis 5 val = 1 : enable val = 0 : disable E[val] : enable endstop val = 1 : enable axis 5 endstop val = 0 : disable axis 5 endstop I[val] : set invert endstop logic level val = 1 : axis 5 endstop invert val = 0 : axis 5 endstop non-invert S[val] : (unit/s) homing speed R[val] : (unit) distance to back away from the endstop during homing U[val] : (step/unit) set step/unit parameter P[val] : (unit) set max position Q[val] : (unit) set min position H[val] : (unit) set home position A[val] : (unit/s²) maximum acceleration J[val] : (unit/s³) maximum jerk F[val] : (unit/s) maximum velocity Example ¶ M61 D1 E1 I0 S15 R5 U8.333 P178 Q0 H45 A4000 J900000 F2000 In this example, R5 sets a 5-unit homing back-off distance. Use configuration values appropriate for the connected axis. M62 - Set Axis 6 Parameters ¶ Descriptions ¶ Configure axis 6 and save its configuration to EEPROM. Units are degrees for a rotary axis or millimeters for a linear axis, according to the steps-per-unit setting. Usage ¶ M62 [D<val>] [E<val>] [I<val>] [S<val>] [R<val>] [U<val>] [P<val>] [Q<val>] [H<val>] [A<val>] [J<val>] [F<val>] Parameter ¶ D[val] : enable axis 6 val = 1 : enable val = 0 : disable E[val] : enable endstop val = 1 : enable axis 6 endstop val = 0 : disable axis 6 endstop I[val] : set invert endstop logic level val = 1 : axis 6 endstop invert val = 0 : axis 6 endstop non-invert S[val] : (unit/s) homing speed R[val] : (unit) distance to back away from the endstop during homing U[val] : (step/unit) set step/unit parameter P[val] : (unit) set max position Q[val] : (unit) set min position H[val] : (unit) set home position A[val] : (unit/s²) maximum acceleration J[val] : (unit/s³) maximum jerk F[val] : (unit/s) maximum velocity Example ¶ M62 D1 E1 I0 S15 R5 U8.333 P178 Q0 H45 A4000 J900000 F2000 In this example, R5 sets a 5-unit homing back-off distance. Use configuration values appropriate for the connected axis. M84 - Disable Steppers ¶ Descriptions ¶ This command can be used to disable steppers. Usage ¶ M84 M100 - Set Auto Feedback Position ¶ Descriptions ¶ Configure automatic position reports and their destination port. Usage ¶ M100 [A<mode>] [B<time>] [C<port>] Parameter ¶ A[mode] : reporting mode. 0 : disable reports. 1 : report during movement, plus the final position when movement completes. 2 : report periodically during movement and while idle. B[time] : report interval in milliseconds. Use at least 10 ; a value below 10 disables reporting. C[port] : destination port. 0 : USB0. 1 : RS232. 3 : USB1. 4 : Ethernet (RJ45). RS485 ( C2 ) is rejected with Unknown: This function cannot be used on RS485! . Open the selected port before requesting reports on it. Each report starts with Position: , followed by X/Y/Z and the positions of enabled W/U/V axes in that order. Values have two decimal places. Example ¶ M100 A1 B200 C0 ; Report position on USB0 every 200 ms during movement, plus the final position. Example report with auxiliary axes disabled: Position:0.00,0.00,-750.00 To report every 200 ms even while idle: M100 A2 B200 C0 To stop automatic position reports: M100 A0 C0 M203 - Set Jerk ¶ Descriptions ¶ Set movement jerk of end effector. Usage ¶ M203 J<value> Parameters ¶ Parameter Description J[value] (mm/s³) required jerk value. Omitting J returns Unknown:Gcode wrong! . Example ¶ M203 J1200000 ;set jerk = 1.200.000 mm/s^3 M204 - Set Max Acceleration ¶ Descriptions ¶ Set movement acceleration. Usage ¶ M204 A<value> Parameters ¶ Parameter Description A[value] (mm/s²) required end-effector acceleration. Omitting A returns Unknown:Gcode wrong! . Example ¶ M204 A15000 ;set accel = 15000 mm/s^2 M205 - Set Begin/End Velocity ¶ Descriptions ¶ Set both the start and end velocity of a movement segment to the same value. Usage ¶ M205 S<value> Parameters ¶ Parameter Description S[value] (mm/s) required start and end velocity. Omitting S returns Unknown:Gcode wrong! . Example ¶ M205 S40 ; Set both start and end velocity to 40 mm/s. M206 - Set Axis Offset ¶ Descriptions ¶ Set the origin offset used by absolute movement commands. The specified origin must be within the robot’s configured workspace and axis limits. Usage ¶ M206 [X<value>] [Y<value>] [Z<value>] [W<value>] [U<value>] [V<value>] Parameters ¶ Parameter Description X[value] (mm) X offset value. Y[value] (mm) Y offset value. Z[value] (mm) Z offset value. W[value] (unit) W offset value, in the configured axis units. U[value] (unit) U offset value, in the configured axis units. V[value] (unit) V offset value, in the configured axis units. Example ¶ M206 X20 Y-10 Z-750 W0 U0 V0 ; Set the XYZ origin to (20, -10, -750), with zero auxiliary-axis offsets. M207 - Set Z Safe ¶ Descriptions ¶ Set the lowest permitted Z coordinate and save it to EEPROM. A value below the workspace limit is rejected. A value above the home Z coordinate disables the additional Z limit. Usage ¶ M207 Z<value> Parameters ¶ Parameter Description Z[value] (mm) lowest permitted Z coordinate. Always specify Z ; sending M207 without it disables the limit. Example ¶ M207 Z-870 ; Set the lowest permitted Z coordinate to -870 mm. The example requires -870 mm to be within the configured workspace and at or below the home Z coordinate. M210 - Set Theta Movement Parameter ¶ Descriptions ¶ Config theta movement para like speed, accel, jerk, start velocity and end velocity. Usage ¶ M210 [F<value>] [A<value>] [J<value>] [S<value>] [E<value>] Parameters ¶ Parameter Description F[value] (unit/s) speed. A[value] (unit/s^2) accel. J[value] (unit/s^3) jerk. S[value] (unit/s) start velocity. E[value] (unit/s) end velocity. Example ¶ M210 F2000 A4000 J800000 S30 E30 ;set all theta movement para M211 - Set Axis 4 Movement Parameter ¶ Descriptions ¶ Config axis 4 movement para like speed, accel, jerk, start velocity and end velocity. Usage ¶ M211 [F<value>] [A<value>] [J<value>] [S<value>] [E<value>] Parameters ¶ Parameter Description F[value] (unit/s) axis 4 speed. A[value] (unit/s^2) axis 4 accel. J[value] (unit/s^3) axis 4 jerk. S[value] (unit/s) start velocity. E[value] (unit/s) end velocity. Example ¶ M211 F2000 A4000 J800000 S30 E30 ;config axis 4 move para M212 - Set Axis 5 Movement Parameter ¶ Descriptions ¶ Config axis 5 movement para like speed, accel, jerk, start velocity and end velocity. Usage ¶ M212 [F<value>] [A<value>] [J<value>] [S<value>] [E<value>] Parameters ¶ Parameter Description F[value] (unit/s) axis 5 speed. A[value] (unit/s^2) axis 5 accel. J[value] (unit/s^3) axis 5 jerk. S[value] (unit/s) start velocity. E[value] (unit/s) end velocity. Example ¶ M212 F2000 A4000 J800000 S30 E30 ;config axis 5 move para M213 - Set Axis 6 Movement Parameter ¶ Descriptions ¶ Config axis 6 movement para like speed, accel, jerk, start velocity and end velocity. Usage ¶ M213 [F<value>] [A<value>] [J<value>] [S<value>] [E<value>] Parameters ¶ Parameter Description F[value] (unit/s) axis 6 speed. A[value] (unit/s^2) axis 6 accel. J[value] (unit/s^3) axis 6 jerk. S[value] (unit/s) start velocity. E[value] (unit/s) end velocity. Example ¶ M213 F2000 A4000 J800000 S30 E30 ;config axis 6 move para M220 - Get Current Axis Parameter ¶ Descriptions ¶ Read the current movement parameters of one axis group. Omitting I selects the Theta group ( I0 ). Usage ¶ M220 [I<val>] Parameter ¶ I[val] : axis index val = 0 : get theta parameter val = 1 : get axis 4 parameter val = 2 : get axis 5 parameter val = 3 : get axis 6 parameter The Theta group uses response labels F , A , J , S , and E . Axis 4 uses WF , WA , WJ , WS , and WE ; axes 5 and 6 use the corresponding U and V prefixes. The selected auxiliary axis must be enabled. Example ¶ M220 I1 ; Read axis 4 movement parameters. Example response for an enabled W axis configured with these values: WF:2000.00 WA:4000.00 WJ:800000.00 WS:30.00 WE:30.00 M500 - Save Settings ¶ Descriptions ¶ Save the current motion parameters and supported configuration settings to EEPROM. Usage ¶ M500 Example ¶ M500 ;Save settings M501 - Reset Settings ¶ Descriptions ¶ Reset settings to the firmware defaults and immediately save them to EEPROM. This overwrites the previously saved settings; an additional M500 is unnecessary. Usage ¶ M501 Example ¶ M501 ; Reset settings to firmware defaults and save them to EEPROM. M502 - Load Settings ¶ Descriptions ¶ Reload the saved motion parameters and supported configuration settings from EEPROM. Usage ¶ M502 Example ¶ M502 ; Reload the settings saved in EEPROM. M600 - Enable Emergency Stop Button ¶ Descriptions ¶ Enable emergency-stop monitoring on two digital inputs and save the selection to EEPROM. Usage ¶ M600 [A<pin>] [B<pin>] A<pin> : first digital input index, 0 – 5 (I0–I5). B<pin> : second digital input index, 0 – 5 (I0–I5). Use the input numbers for the connected emergency-stop circuit. Example ¶ M600 A4 B5 ; Enable emergency-stop monitoring on inputs I4 and I5. M601 - Disable Emergency Stop Button ¶ Descriptions ¶ Disable E_STOP button. docs.text: The G0 and G1 commands add a linear MOVE to the queue to be performed after all previous moves are completed. Set F (feed rate), A (acceleration), J (jerk), S (start velocity), and E (end velocity) once. Subsequent movement commands use these settings until changed; motion parameters omitted from a command keep their current settings.
docs.title: Descriptions

docs.text: G1 [X<pos>] [Y<pos>] [Z<pos>] [W<angle>] [U<angle>] [V<angle>] [F<val>] [A<val>] [J<val>] [S<val>] [E<val>]
docs.title: Usage

docs.text: Parameter Description X[pos] (mm) A coordinate on the X-axis. Y[pos] (mm) A coordinate on the Y-axis. Z[pos] (mm) A coordinate on the Z-axis. W[angle] (unit) Axis 4 position. U[angle] (unit) Axis 5 position. V[angle] (unit) Axis 6 position. F[val] (mm/s) The maximum movement rate of the move between the start and endpoint. The feedrate set here applies to subsequent moves that omit this parameter. A[val] (mm/s2) Acceleration of the motion. J[val] (mm/s3) Jerk of the motion. S[val] (mm/s) Begin velocity. E[val] (mm/s) Finish velocity. For W/U/V, a unit is a degree for a rotary axis or a millimeter for a linear axis, according to its steps-per-unit configuration.
docs.title: Parameters

docs.text: G01 F1500 A15000 J550000 S100 E100 ; Set the feed rate to 1500 mm/s, acceleration to 15000 mm/s², jerk to 550000 mm/s³, start velocity to 100 mm/s, and end velocity to 100 mm/s. G01 X0 Y0 Z-750 ; Move to the absolute position (X0, Y0, Z-750). G01 X50 ; Move to X = 50 mm. G01 W90 ; Rotate to 90° on the 4-axis
docs.title: Example

docs.text: G2 adds a clockwise arc move to the planner; G3 adds a counter-clockwise arc. The arc runs in the XY plane from the current position to the specified X/Y endpoint, keeping Z unchanged. I and J locate the center relative to the arc’s starting point.
docs.title: Descriptions

docs.text: G02 I<offset> J<offset> [X<pos>] [Y<pos>] [W<angle>] [U<angle>] [V<angle>] [F<val>] [A<val>] [S<val>] [E<val>] Use G03 for a counter-clockwise arc. Always include both I and J , even when one offset is zero. In these commands, J is the Y center offset; the previously configured jerk remains in use.
docs.title: Usage

docs.text: Parameter Description I[offset] (mm) Required X offset from the starting point to the arc center. J[offset] (mm) Required Y offset from the starting point to the arc center. X[pos] (mm) A coordinate on the X-axis. Y[pos] (mm) A coordinate on the Y-axis. W[angle] , U[angle] , V[angle] :(unit) Axis 4, 5, and 6 positions, using the configured units for each axis. F[val] (mm/s) The maximum movement rate of the move between the start and endpoint. The feedrate set here applies to subsequent moves that omit this parameter. A[val] (mm/s2) Acceleration of the motion. S[val] (mm/s) Begin velocity. E[val] (mm/s) Finish velocity.
docs.title: Parameters

docs.text: G28 ; Home all axes. G90 ; Use absolute positioning. G01 X50 Y0 Z-750 F200 ; Move to the arc start at (X50, Y0, Z-750). G02 X0 Y-50 I-50 J0 F200 ; Clockwise 90° arc around (X0, Y0), radius 50 mm. G03 X50 Y0 I0 J50 F200 ; Counter-clockwise 90° arc back to (X50, Y0). Both arcs keep Z at -750 mm. The X/Y endpoints are absolute positions; I/J are offsets from each arc’s starting point to the center at (X0, Y0).

docs.text: G6 [X<angle>] [Y<angle>] [Z<angle>] [W<pos>] [U<pos>] [R<pos>] [F<val>] [A<val>] [J<val>] [S<val>] [E<val>]
docs.title: Usage

docs.text: Parameter Description X[angle] (degree) The value of the Theta 1 angle. Y[angle] (degree) The value of the Theta 2 angle. Z[angle] (degree) The value of the Theta 3 angle. W[pos] (unit) Axis 4 position. U[pos] (unit) Axis 5 position. R[pos] (unit) Axis 6 position. F[val] (mm/s) Cartesian feed rate. A[val] (mm/s²) Cartesian acceleration. J[val] (mm/s³) Cartesian jerk. S[val] (mm/s) Start velocity. E[val] (mm/s) End velocity. W/U/R use the configured units for their axes: degrees for rotary axes or millimeters for linear axes. Omitted F/A/J/S/E values keep their current motion settings, which also apply to subsequent moves until changed.

M03, M04 - Set Digital Output / PWM

docs.text: Set digital output states or PWM values. M03 uses 8-bit PWM values; M04 uses 16-bit PWM values. Both commands can set digital outputs with D .
docs.title: Descriptions

docs.text: M03 D<pin> W<state> M04 D<pin> W<state> M03 P<pin> W<value> M04 P<pin> W<value>
docs.title: Usage

docs.text: Parameter Values and function D<pin> Digital output index: 0 – 7 . Use W1 to turn it on or W0 to turn it off. P<pin> PWM output index: 0 – 7 . W<value> with M03 P... 8-bit PWM value: 0 – 255 . W<value> with M04 P... 16-bit PWM value: 0 – 65535 . Always include W , including for digital outputs. Several outputs can be selected on one line, such as M03 D0 D1 W1 . D and P select digital or PWM control of the output with that index.
docs.title: Parameters

docs.text: M03 D0 W1 ; Turn on digital output D0. M03 D1 D2 W1 ; Turn on digital outputs D1 and D2. M03 P3 W128 ; Set PWM output P3 to 128 on the 8-bit scale (0–255). M04 P4 W32768 ; Set PWM output P4 to 32768 on the 16-bit scale (0–65535). M03 D0 W0 ; Turn off digital output D0. Each command returns Ok .
docs.title: Example
M05 - Turn Off Digital Output / PWM

docs.text: Turn off selected digital outputs or set selected PWM outputs to zero.
docs.title: Descriptions

docs.text: M05 D<pin> M05 P<pin>
docs.title: Usage

docs.text: Parameter Values and function D<pin> Digital output index: 0 – 7 . Set the selected output to OFF. P<pin> PWM output index: 0 – 7 . Set the selected PWM value to zero. Several outputs can be selected on one line. Specify at least one D or P output; a bare M05 does not select all outputs.
docs.title: Parameters

docs.text: M03 D0 W1 ; Turn on digital output D0. M05 D0 ; Turn off digital output D0. M03 P1 W128 ; Set PWM output P1 to 128 on the 8-bit scale. M05 P1 ; Set PWM output P1 to zero. M05 D2 D3 P4 ; Turn off D2 and D3, and set PWM output P4 to zero. Each command returns Ok .
docs.title: Example

docs.text: Read the current state of selected digital inputs or the raw ADC values of selected analog inputs. Several digital and analog channels can be requested on one line.

docs.text: Response Meaning I<pin> V<value> Digital input state: 0 or 1 . A<pin> V<value> Raw 12-bit ADC value: 0 – 4095 . One response is returned per selected input when the I/O board replies. Specify at least one input from the ranges above.

docs.text: Configure automatic input reports. Digital inputs report state changes; analog inputs report sampled values at the requested interval.
docs.title: Descriptions

docs.text: M08 I<pin> [B<enable>] [P<port>] M08 A<pin> [C<period_us>] [P<port>]
docs.title: Usage

docs.text: Parameter Values and function I<pin> Digital input index: 0 – 5 . Several inputs can be selected on one line. B<enable> Digital reports: 1 enables reporting; 0 disables it. Default: 1 when omitted. A<pin> Analog input index: 0 or 1 . Both channels can be selected on one line. C<period_us> Requested analog report period in microseconds. Default: 500000 (500 ms) when omitted. The I/O-board firmware determines the supported minimum period and the value used to disable analog reports. P<port> Report destination: 0 = USB0, 1 = RS232, 2 = RS485, 3 = USB1. The startup report destination is USB0. Open the selected serial port before requesting reports on it. RS485 ( P2 ) requires full-duplex mode; half-duplex mode returns Unknown: This function cannot be used on RS485! . Ethernet ( P4 ) is not accepted by M08 . Digital inputs assigned to an enabled emergency stop are used for E-stop monitoring instead of ordinary automatic digital reports.
docs.title: Parameters

docs.text: Each configuration command returns Ok . Reports then arrive as: Response Meaning I<pin> V<value> Digital input state: 0 or 1 . A<pin> V<value> Raw 12-bit ADC value: 0 – 4095 .
docs.title: Feedback

docs.text: M08 I3 B1 P0 ; Report changes on digital input I3 through USB0. M08 A1 C500000 P0 ; Request analog input A1 reports every 500 ms through USB0. Example automatic reports; values depend on the connected signals: I3 V0 A1 V2478 To stop automatic reports for digital input I3: M08 I3 B0 ; Disable automatic reports for digital input I3.

docs.text: Configure automatic position reports and their destination port.
docs.title: Descriptions

docs.text: M100 [A<mode>] [B<time>] [C<port>]
docs.title: Usage

docs.text: A[mode] : reporting mode. 0 : disable reports. 1 : report during movement, plus the final position when movement completes. 2 : report periodically during movement and while idle. B[time] : report interval in milliseconds. Use at least 10 ; a value below 10 disables reporting. C[port] : destination port. 0 : USB0. 1 : RS232. 3 : USB1. 4 : Ethernet (RJ45). RS485 ( C2 ) is rejected with Unknown: This function cannot be used on RS485! . Open the selected port before requesting reports on it. Each report starts with Position: , followed by X/Y/Z and the positions of enabled W/U/V axes in that order. Values have two decimal places.

docs.text: USEFUL COMMANDS ¶ Identify Delta Robot Command ¶ To check if a COM port is connected to a Delta Robot, send the command IsDelta . If connected, it replies with YesDelta . The baudrate should be 115200. IsDelta >>> YesDelta Model: Delta X 1 , Delta X 2 , Delta X 3 , Delta X S . Disconnect COM Port Command ¶ Send Disconnect when ending a control session. Disconnect On Delta X 3 , this updates the connection state and indicator. Close the COM port in your host application to release the serial connection. Model: Delta X 1 , Delta X 2 , Delta X 3 , Delta X S . Get Current Position Command ¶ To retrieve the robot’s current end-effector position, use the Position command. The response format depends on the model. Delta X 1 / Delta X 2 / Delta X S Position >>> X30.4 Y90 Z-800 W50 U90 Delta X 3 returns X,Y,Z in mm, with two decimal places, calculated from emitted motor steps. The coordinates use the robot’s base frame, without the working origin set by M206 ; W/U are not included. G93 returns the same position. Position >>> 31.00,43.00,-291.00 Run G28 before using Position , PositionOffset , or Angle on X3. If the XYZ reference is unknown, these commands return Error:XYZ position is unknown; home with G28. Model: Delta X 1 , Delta X 2 , Delta X 3 , Delta X S . Get Position Offset Command ¶ Use PositionOffset to query position information related to the working offset. Its meaning and response format depend on the model. Delta X 1 / Delta X 2 / Delta X S PositionOffset >>> X0.5 Y1.2 Z-2.2 Delta X 3 returns the current XYZ position relative to the working origin set by M206 , in mm with two decimal places. At the working origin, the response is: PositionOffset >>> 0.00,0.00,0.00 With no working origin enabled, X3 returns the same coordinates as Position . Model: Delta X 1 , Delta X 2 , Delta X 3 , Delta X S . Get Current Theta Angles ¶ For the current angles of the three upper arms, use Angle (angles in deg). Delta X 1 / Delta X 2 / Delta X S Angle >>> X2.46 Y2.46 Z2.46 Delta X 3 returns Theta1,Theta2,Theta3 in degrees, with two decimal places: Angle >>> 2.46,2.46,2.46 Model: Delta X 1 , Delta X 2 , Delta X 3 , Delta X S . Get Current Endstop Sensor States ¶ Read the current states of the three home sensors. HTs >>> 111 Model: Delta X 1 , Delta X 2 , Delta X 3 , Delta X S . Get Robot IMEI ¶ To find the robot’s unique IMEI, use the IMEI command. Delta X 1 / Delta X 2 / Delta X S IMEI >>> 0004-0000-0000-0012 Delta X 3 includes the IMEI: prefix: IMEI >>> IMEI:0002-0000-0001 Model: Delta X 1 , Delta X 2 , Delta X 3 , Delta X S . Get Robot Information ¶ The Infor command provides details like the model, mainboard version, and firmware version. Delta X S example Infor >>> @IMWI Technology >>> Main_board_version: V1.0 >>> Firmware_version: V1.0 >>> Model: DELTA_XS_V4_D800 Delta X 3 example Infor >>> @Delta X Robotics >>> Main_board_version: V1.02 >>> Firmware_version: 1.08 >>> Model: DELTA_X_3 Model: Delta X 1 , Delta X 2 , Delta X 3 , Delta X S . Get Robot Active Status ¶ To check the robot’s current status, use DeltaState . Delta X 2: Free , Running , Wait , Almostdone , Done . Delta X 3: Free , Running , Wait , Executed , Done , Stop , SendConfirm . DeltaState >>> Free Model: Delta X 2 , Delta X 3 . Set Feedback String ¶ You can customize the feedback message after a command execution by setting a feedback string. Delta X S Feedback: done >>> set feedback string to 'done' Delta X 3 uses uppercase FEEDBACK: followed immediately by 1 to 24 printable ASCII characters. Send this while the robot is idle. The setting is saved to EEPROM, and the reply uses the new string: FEEDBACK:done >>> done Model: Delta X 3 , Delta X S . With Delta X 2 model, this command will be FEEDBACK:<custom_string> . Emergency Stop Command ¶ Send an emergency signal with Emergency:<state> . States include Reset, Stop, Pause, or Resume. Emergency:<state> Where <state> can be: Reset - reset robot Stop - stop robot Pause - pause robot Resume - resume robot On Delta X 3 and Delta X S V4/V5 , use the exact forms Emergency:Stop , Emergency:Pause , Emergency:Resume , and Emergency:Reset , with no space after the colon. Stop and Pause interrupt the current movement. Resume clears the software stop/pause condition; it does not continue the interrupted path. Check pending commands before resuming, because Stop does not guarantee that the queue is cleared. For the recovery sequence, queue handling, and controller restart steps, see Emergency stop and recovery in Termite . Model: Delta X 2 , Delta X 3 , Delta X S . Get Current Temperature ¶ To get the hot end’s current temperature, use the TempState command. Model: Delta X 2 TempState >>> T:27.3 Model: Delta X 1 Temp >>> T:28.2 Model: Delta X 2 Set up WIFI connection ¶ For models Delta X 1 and Delta X 2 , use the SSID and PSWD commands to connect to Wi-Fi. The robot will return its IP address upon successful connection. Make sure to switch to WiFi mode . SSID:<wifi_name> PSWD:<wifi_password> IP For Eg: SSID:IMWI wifi >>> Ok PSWD:onlyuknow >>> Ok >>> IP:192.168.233.1 If you forgot your IP: IP >>> IP:192.168.233.1 Model: Delta X 1 , Delta X 2 . docs.text: G-CODE MACRO PROGRAMMING ¶ GOTO - Jumping Ahead in G-CODE ¶ Description ¶ GOTO is pretty simple to use, just followed by the sequence number ( N number) you would like to jump to. Example ¶ This program snippet uses a GOTO which address is 15 to jump over N10 and go directly to N15 Conditional Expresssions ¶ Let’s talk about the rules for Conditional Expressions. Here are the rules: Conditional expressions must be enclosed in square brackets (“[” and “]”). A Conditional Expression consists of two operands and a comparison operator. An operand may be a # variable or a number. There must be a space between a comparison operator and operands. Comparison Operators: EQ : Equal == : Equal NE : not equal != : not equal GT : greater than > : greater than GE : greater than or equal >= : greater than or equal LT : less than < : less than LE : less than or equal <= : less than or equal Comparisons may be further grouped with square brackets and AND, OR, or XOR. Example: ¶ [[0 LE #100] AND [#100 LE 1000]] [[0 < #100] AND [#100 > 1000]] (True if the value of #100 is 0 to 1000) Math Methods ¶ #sin([value]) - Compute sine (value is degree) #cos([value]) - Compute cosine (value is degree) #cos([value]) - Compute cosine (value is degree) #tan([value]) - Compute tangent (value is degree) #asin([value]) - Compute arc sine(result is degree) #atan([value]) - Compute arc tangent (result is degree) #atan2(x, y) - Compute arc tangent with two parameters (result is degree) #abs([value]) - Compute absolute value #sqrt([value]) - Compute square root #pow([value1],[value2]) - Raise to power, ex: #result = #pow(2,3) -----> #result = 8 If conditional Branching ¶ While GOTO represents an “unconditional branch” in G-Code execution, IF allows for “conditional branching”. Usage ¶ IF [Conditional Expression] THEN <do somethings> If Conditional Expression is true , the G-code will execute the command behind THEN. If Conditional Expression is false , the G-code falls through to the next line. Example ¶ IF [#100 GE 200] THEN GOTO 15 ;//if #100 >= 200 then GOTO N15 Variables ¶ Description ¶ They can be assigned values, and its value could be changed during program execution. When you refer to them, they give back the last value they were assigned. The syntax for a variable is the pound sign followed by a number up to however many digits your controller supports that identifies the variable. For example, we can write “#100 = 0” to assign the value “0” to the variable “#100”. Usage ¶ Global Variables : When a variabel is prefixed with #GLOBAL_ like #GLOBAL_IsRunning , the program of other robots in the project will be able to use that variable. System Variables : #X, #Y, #Z, #W, #U, #V - Current robot position #F, #A, #S, #E - Current robot speed, acceleration, start and end speed #ConveyorSpeed, #ConveyorDirection - Speed and direction of the conveyor #O0_X, #O0_Y, #O0_Z, #O0_W, #O0_H - The position and size of the first object detected by the camera. #O[id]_X, #O[id]_Y, #O[id]_Z, #O[id]_W, #O[id]_H - [id] is the order in which the object appears. If the object is deleted, it will have a NULL value. Example: IF [#O0_X != NULL] THEN G01 X[#O0_X] Robot Input : #Response - the string is sent from the robot to the software #I[index] - state of input pin at index Example: G28 >>> Ok => #Response = "Ok" M7 I0 >>> I0 V1 => #Response = "I0 V1", #I0 = 1 M7 I2 >>> I2 V0 => #Response = "I2 V0", #I2 = 0 Subprograms ¶ Define a Subprogram ¶ The syntax to start a subprogram with the letter O followed by a number . This number is the name of the subprogram. As the example above, line 20 is the start of a subprogram named 1000. And then, we start programing for the subprogram (from line 30 to 55). To end the subprogram, we use M99 command (line 65). Call the subprogram ¶ To call the subprogram, we use the syntax: M98 P<name of the subprogram> Example ¶ Execute another G-code file ¶ M98 F<file_name> For example: M98 Fpick_char pick_char is the name of G-code file. Function ¶ Object Detecting Functions ¶ M98 PpauseCamera - Pause reading image frames from the camera. M98 PresumeCamera - Resume reading camera. M98 PcaptureCamera - Capture a frame from camera. M98 PdeleteFirstObject - Delete the first element in the container of the tracking objects. M98 PclearObjects - Clear all tracking objects in container. M98 PsyncConveyor - Synchronize the robot with the conveyor. M98 PstopSyncConveyor - Stop syncing the robot with the conveyor. Communicate ¶ M98 PsendExternalMCU - Send a string to the external microcontroller that is connecting to the software. Eg: M98 PsendExternalMCU("Hello World") Contact Us ¶ Store: https://deltaxstore.com Website: https://www.deltaxrobot.com Email: deltaxrobot@gmail.com Phone: +84 38 875 2005

docs.text: Vision Kit V1 ¶ The Vision Kit V1 by Delta X Robotics is an essential tool for quick deployment of vision-based projects, making it ideal for research and development (R&D), testing, education, and small-scale manufacturing. Designed with versatility and ease of use in mind, this kit is perfect for various industries that require reliable vision solutions. Key Features: ¶ Camera Resolution : 1920x1080 (Full HD) ensures high-quality image capture, suitable for detailed analysis and processing. Type of Shutter : The camera is equipped with a Global Shutter , allowing precise image capturing, particularly useful in fast-moving object detection scenarios. Frame Rate : Supports 30fps at 1080p , offering smooth and real-time video output for efficient data processing. Lens Focal Length : The 4.3mm lens delivers a 70-degree field of view without distortion, making it suitable for capturing wide areas in one frame. Minimum Working Distance : The system operates optimally at a minimum distance of 100 mm , perfect for close-up applications requiring high accuracy. Connection Interface : The kit connects via USB , providing easy integration with computers and other devices for seamless data transfer. Adjustable Lighting : Equipped with a bright LED that can be adjusted using a volume resistor, the kit offers customizable lighting for varying environments. The lighting angle spans 150 degrees , ensuring even illumination, while the cold white LED color ensures clear image capture without color distortion. In the Box: ¶ Vision Kit : Includes a high-resolution camera paired with an adjustable LED lighting system. Power Supply : A 12VDC/3A power adapter for consistent and reliable operation. USB-B Cable : Ensures easy plug-and-play connectivity. Applications: ¶ Vision Kit V1 is an excellent choice for a variety of vision projects, ranging from educational demos to research and small manufacturing. Its robust and adjustable design makes it highly adaptable to various tasks, including object detection, quality inspection, and automation system integration. Priced at $200 , the Vision Kit V1 is a cost-effective, flexible solution for those who need precision and reliability in vision-based projects. Ships directly from Vietnam, ensuring quick delivery worldwide. For additional products like the Industrial Vision System or the Delta X 1 Develop Kit , explore our store to find the best fit for your robotics and automation needs.

docs.text: Delta X S Assembly Guide ¶ Introduction ¶ Welcome to the Delta X S Robot Manual. This guide will help you assemble your Delta X S robot arm step by step. Please read and follow the instructions carefully to ensure safe and proper assembly. Safety Precautions ¶ Ensure that you are working in a clean and well-ventilated area. Wear appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) such as safety goggles and gloves. Turn off and unplug the robot arm before starting to repair the robot. Package Contents ¶ Before you begin, make sure you have received all the components listed in the package: Assembly Instructions ¶ Before mounting the Delta robot, ensure that the frame or surface you are attaching it to is stable and level. Use a measuring tape and a level to verify the frame’s position. Step 1: Mounting the robot onto the frame ¶ On the base of the robot body, there are four Ø8 holes used for attaching the Delta robot body to the frame. Please use M8 bolts to tighten and secure the robot. Step 2: Power on and Home the robot ¶ Power on the robot ¶ Plug in the Robot Power Cable: Connect the power cable from the power supply unit to the robot’s power input port. Ensure a secure connection. Turn on the Power Supply: Switch the power button on the power supply unit. You should see the power LED confirming that power is flowing. Home the robot ¶ Connect the Robot with a Computer: using USB-B cable to the USB0 port on the backside of the robot body. Control robot with Delta X Software : Download the software at our download page address Press Connect button and wait for connection. If the connection is successful, try the Home button, the robot will go home and the first move is done. Step 3: Attaching the arms to the robot body ¶ Mounting the Upper Arms to the flanges: DO NOT attempt to rotate the flange if the upper arm is not installed. Use 6x M6x16mm bolts to assemble the upper arm onto the flange, ensuring that the marked surfaces align with each other. Install the Lower Arms and the Moving Base : Pull the lower arm out and position it on the outside of the ball end of the upper arm. Repeat this process with the other two arms. Do the same with moving base: Step 4(Optional): Install Axis 4 (5,6) ¶ If the robot has axis 4, assemble the universal joint of axis 4 onto the rotating flange underneath the robot body, ensuring a snug fit. Then, tighten the M3 bolt securely first and then fasten the hex socket set screw M3 . And the basic assembly of the robot is now complete. Input & Output Connection ¶ Digital INPUT pins (24VDC/3mA) & Analog input pins(0-10VDC/0-4096): INPUT PIN Pin 1 - I0 Pin 6 - A0 Pin 2 - I1 Pin 7 - A1 Pin 3 - I2 Pin 8 - 24V Pin 4 - I3 Pin 9 - GND Pin 5 - GND Digital OUPUT pins (24VDC/500mA): OUTPUT PIN Pin 1 - D0 Pin 2 - D1 Pin 3 - D2 Pin 4 - D3 Pin 5 - D4 Pin 6 - D5 Pin 7 - D6 Pin 8 - D7 Pin 9~12 - 24VDC Pin 12~15 - GND E-STOP pins: E-STOP PIN Pin 1 - GND Pin 2 - I4 Pin 3 - I5 Pin 4 - 24V Input Terminal Adapter (DB9 Male) and Wiring Example ¶ Output Terminal Adapter (DB15 Male) and Wiring Example ¶ Caution ¶ Connect any output as shown above, do not load more than 500mA for each output pin. Do not connect any output pin to 24V. Maintenance ¶ Proper maintenance is crucial to ensure the longevity and optimal performance of your Delta Robot. Here are some key maintenance considerations: DO NOT expose the robot body, its components, or electronics to direct water or moisture. Water damage can affect the functionality and safety of the robot. Always work in a dry environment. Keep the robot and its components clean by wiping down surfaces with a soft, dry cloth. Power off the robot when not in use for an extended period. Periodically inspect and tighten all bolts, nuts, and connectors to prevent loosening due to vibrations or movements. By following these maintenance practices, you can maximize the lifespan and efficiency of your Delta Robot while minimizing downtime and potential issues. Always refer to the user manual for specific maintenance guidelines provided by the manufacturer. docs.text: Delta X S Frame Assembly Guide ¶ Introduction ¶ This guide provides detailed instructions on how to assemble a frame. You will be guided through each step to ensure a successful frame assembly process. Requirements ¶ Before getting started, make sure you have the following tools and materials: Frame components (including individual parts as listed below) Hexagon Tool & other assembly accessories Step 1: Preparation ¶ 1.1. Review the manufacturer’s assembly manual to understand the specific steps. 1.2. Arrange and inspect the frame parts to ensure nothing is missing or damaged. 1.3. Ensure you have all the necessary tools and materials ready for assembly. Step 2: Frame Assembly ¶ Place the frame on a suitable work surface. Use assembly tools to connect the frame components in the appropriate order. Follow these steps: 2.1 Installing the Corner Brackets ¶ Install M8 T-nut(8) first, then place the 4040 corner bracket (5) onto the aluminum profile (1), ensuring a proper fit and alignment. Then use a hex wrench to secure the corner bracket to the aluminum profile. Tighten the screws to firmly attach the corner bracket to the beam. NOTE: Use M8x15mm Bolts(6) and DON’T forget to install M8 Washer(7) in every joints. 2.2. Install the rectangular frame below ¶ Prepare the two edges of the rectangular frame as follows, DON’T forget to insert 8x M8 T-nut(8) . Then complete the rect by adding 2 remaining edges. 2.3 Adding 4 Support Columns to the Frame ¶ Position the first support column at its designated location near one corner of the frame. Align the support column vertically and ensure it is plumb using a level or other suitable measuring tool. Attach the support column to the frame using 2x 4040 Corner Brackets(5) on the 2 sides as the 2 edges of the rectangular frame below. Ensure a secure and stable connection. Adding Diagonal Braces for Frame Reinforcement: use 4040 Angled Brackets 135deg (4) and Corner Alu(3) to create diagonal braces for the frame. This step uses M8x20mm Bolts(9) , M8 Washer(7) and M8 T-nut(8) . Repeat these steps for the remaining 3 support columns, placing one near each corner of the frame and we got this one: Adding Top Diagonal Braces: as a part of frame reinforcement, we will add more some diagonal braces to the frame. 2.4 Create Top Rectangular Frame with Crossbars for Robot Mounting ¶ Create a rect frame like the rect below and then add 2 middle crossbars, follow these dimensions for model Delta X S D600 and Delta X S D800 . 2.5 Install Top Rectangular Frame with the Main Frame Body ¶ Flip the Top Rectangular Frame, position the main frame body components within the rectangular frame, ensuring they fit securely. Adding Bolts and Washers and ensure a firm connection throughout the frame. Step 3: Finalizing the Assembly ¶ Inspect the entire frame assembly to ensure all components are securely attached and aligned. Test the stability and structural integrity of the frame by applying gentle pressure or shaking. Make any necessary adjustments if there are signs of instability. docs.text: CONTROLING DELTA X 2 ROBOT WITH ARDUINO ¶ This tutorial will guide you on using an Arduino board to control the Delta X 2 robot draw a spiral through the Serial Port beside the main USB port on the robot body. Prerequisites: Delta X 2 Robot Kit Arduino Board (e.g., Arduino Pro Mini, Arduino Uno) USB Cable Any Arduino IDE installed on your computer (this tutorial use Visual Code with PlatformIO extension). A button and wires. USB to TTL module. Step 1: Wiring Diagram ¶ Step 2: Write the Sketch for Arduino ¶ The idea is when the button pressed, the Arduino will create a G-code queue and send it via Serial Port to control the robot drawing the spiral. You can visit my Github to DOWNLOAD the project . To calculate the spiral dimensions, you need to consider both the working range of the robot and the specifications of your own system. Please exercise caution when identifying the z_safe value, ensuring that the end effector does not come into contact with any obstacles along its path. Programming ¶ First, we create queues to store G-codes. #include <Arduino.h> #include "Vector/Vector.h" String GcodeArray[20]; String InitGcodeArray[20]; Vector<String> InitGcodeQueue; Vector<String> GcodeQueue; Create init G-code queue, this queue code includes initialization commands, homing, setting feedrate and acceleration, and more. void create_init_gcode_queue() { InitGcodeQueue.push_back("G28"); InitGcodeQueue.push_back("M203 S" + String((int)feedrate)); InitGcodeQueue.push_back("M204 A" + String((int)accel)); InitGcodeQueue.push_back("M205 S" + String(begin_vel)); InitGcodeQueue.push_back("M360 E0"); InitGcodeQueue.push_back("G01 X0 Y0 Z" + String(z_safe)); } Calculate and create a spiral queue: void create_gcode_queue(int start_radius, int stop_radius, int step) { GcodeQueue.push_back("M03"); GcodeQueue.push_back("G01 X" + String(start_radius) + " Y0 Z" + String(z_exe)); int current_x = start_radius; int current_i = start_radius; String gc = ""; while (abs(current_x) <= stop_radius - step) { if (current_x > 0) { current_i = -current_x - step / 2; current_x = -current_x - step; } else { current_i = -current_x + step / 2; current_x = -current_x + step; } gc = "G02 X" + String(current_x) + " Y0 I" + String(current_i) + " J0"; GcodeQueue.push_back(gc); } GcodeQueue.push_back("M05"); GcodeQueue.push_back("G01 X0 Y0 Z" + String(z_safe)); } Then check the button pressing event in loop function: void loop() { if (millis() - lastMillis >= 200) { lastMillis = millis(); if (!digitalRead(2)) { if (stt == FREE) { stt = EXECUTING; create_gcode_queue(start_radius, stop_radius, step); send_exe_gcodes(); } } } ... } Conclusion ¶ Controlling the Delta X 2 robot using Arduino or any device that supports Serial Port communication is straightforward and versatile. Whether you are working with Arduino or other compatible devices, the provided code serves as a foundation for implementing and customizing control functionalities for the Delta X 2 robot within diverse automation applications.

docs.text: DeltaXStudio — System Setup ¶ Start by connecting the robot to your network and checking its hardware. Then continue with Calibration , Vision , and Pick & Place . For custom programs, use the separate Blockly guide . Connect to the robot for the first time ¶ Power on the robot and its controller, then wait for the robot’s Wi-Fi access point (AP) to appear. On your computer or tablet, open the Wi-Fi list and join the robot’s AP. Its name normally follows DeltaXSmart-xxxx . The default password is 12345678 ; use the configured password if it has been changed. Stay connected even if your device reports that this network has no Internet access. Open http://deltax.com in your browser. DeltaXStudio should appear as shown below. Connect the robot to your Wi-Fi ¶ Open WiFi at the upper left of DeltaXStudio, then use Scan WiFi to find and select your network. Enter your Wi-Fi password and click Connect . Wait for the connection to succeed. At the top of the window, check that Connected WiFi shows your network name and Local IP shows an IP address. Write down Local IP before switching your computer to another network. In this screenshot, the robot has joined Delta X Lab_5G and its Local IP is 192.168.50.231 . Your network name and IP address will be different. Use Local IP for access through your Wi-Fi; the address under Access belongs to the robot’s AP. Open DeltaXStudio through your Wi-Fi ¶ Connect your computer or tablet to the same Wi-Fi network as the robot. In your browser, enter http://<Local IP>:3000 , replacing <Local IP> with the address you wrote down. For the screenshot above, the address is http://192.168.50.231:3000 . Confirm that DeltaXStudio opens. You can now access the robot through your own network. The standard web port is 3000 ; use the port supplied with your installation if it differs. After switching to your Wi-Fi, use the robot’s IP address instead of deltax.com . Once IP access works, you can turn off Enable AP in the WiFi window if you no longer need the robot’s hotspot. Find the main controls ¶ Once connected, use the navigation to work through the setup: Area Use Dashboard View the robot, camera, conveyor, and operating status. Settings → System Configure the installed hardware, robot, vision, and startup behavior. Settings → Calibration Run the guided camera and robot calibration. Settings → Parameters Set pick and place positions, motion parameters, and object selections. Vision Capture images for labeling and training in DeltaXHub, or prepare template images for detection. Programs Create, check, save, and run Blockly tasks. Keep Auto Start disabled while setting up the system. After changing settings, click Save and wait for confirmation. When a configuration change requires a restart, stop the running task first, then use Settings → System → System Control → Reset and wait for the interface to reconnect. Check the installed hardware ¶ Open Settings → System and review Hardware Settings . Enable the devices actually installed, including the main camera and, for a conveyor setup, the conveyor and encoder. Check the installed camera, encoder, conveyor, and tool outputs. The selected devices and numeric values are examples; use the hardware fitted to your installation. In Robot Settings , check the robot model and its detected address. The robot address identifies the robot controller; it is separate from the Wi-Fi Local IP used to open the web page. Check the end-effector type and output configuration for your vacuum tool or gripper. Verify the model and controller address for each robot. This address is separate from the web interface IP. Save the settings and return to Dashboard . Confirm that the intended robot is connected and that the camera produces a current image. For a conveyor system, confirm that encoder readings respond to conveyor movement before starting calibration. A working web page confirms access to DeltaXStudio; check the device status separately before sending robot commands. If an advanced setting is hidden, switch the settings view from Basic to Advanced . Ready for calibration ¶ Continue when the intended robot and camera respond correctly, and the encoder responds to conveyor movement if your setup uses tracking. Then calibrate the camera and robot coordinates . If you cannot connect ¶ Problem What to check The robot AP is missing Check power and wait for the controller to start, then refresh your device’s Wi-Fi list. deltax.com does not open Make sure you are connected to the robot’s AP and enter http://deltax.com explicitly. Stay on the AP if your device warns about no Internet access. The robot cannot join your Wi-Fi Check the selected network and password, move within signal range, and scan again. The AP disconnects during setup Join your own Wi-Fi and find the robot controller’s IP in the router’s connected-device list. The IP address does not open Confirm that your computer and robot are on the same network. Check the current Local IP and include the web port, normally 3000 . A previously working bookmark stops opening Your router may have assigned a new IP address. Check the controller’s current address in the router, or through the robot AP if it is available.

docs.text: Control Delta X 3 and Delta X S with Termite ¶ Use Termite on Windows to send text commands to your robot through its USB serial connection. This guide takes you from selecting the COM port to homing and a short movement test. Before you start ¶ Prepare an assembled, securely mounted robot, its power supply, a USB data cable, and a Windows computer. Clear the robot’s working area before homing or moving it, and keep its physical emergency-stop control accessible. Choose the command reference that matches your robot: Robot G-code reference Delta X 3, firmware < 2.0.0 X3 G-code Delta X 3, firmware > 2.0.0 New firmware reference — being prepared Delta X S V4 XS V4 G-code Delta X S V5 XS V5 G-code The command examples below follow the existing X3 reference and the XS V4/V5 references. For the new X3 firmware, use the commands provided with that firmware until its reference is available. 1. Open Termite ¶ Download Termite from the official CompuPhase download page , install or extract it, and open the application. The large area displays communication with the robot. Type commands in the narrow entry field at the bottom and press Enter to send them. 2. Connect the robot and find its COM port ¶ Connect the robot’s USB control port to the computer with the USB data cable. Robot USB port Computer USB port Turn on the robot’s power supply. USB communication alone does not supply power for robot movement. Close other applications using the robot’s serial port, such as another terminal or control application. Open Windows Device Manager , then expand Ports (COM & LPT) . Note the robot’s COM number. You can unplug and reconnect the USB cable to identify the entry that disappears and returns. This screenshot shows USB-SERIAL CH340 (COM5) . The device name and COM number may differ on your computer; use the port identified for your robot. 3. Configure the serial connection ¶ Click Settings and use these values: Setting Value Port The robot’s COM port from Device Manager Baud rate 115200 Data bits 8 Stop bits 1 Parity none Flow control none Forward none Transmitted text Append CR-LF Local echo Checked, to display the commands you send COM5 is the example port shown in these screenshots. Select the port assigned to your robot in Device Manager. Click OK . If the status still reads Disconnected - click to connect , click that status field to open the port. 4. Check communication ¶ Enter the following command in the bottom field and press Enter : IsDelta The robot should reply with YesDelta . With local echo enabled, your typed command also appears in the receive area; that echoed line alone does not confirm a connection. Then send: Infor Check the returned robot model and firmware version against the reference selected above. 5. Home the robot ¶ Make sure the robot can complete its homing movement, then send: G28 Wait for homing to finish and for the completion reply, normally Ok , before sending a movement command. If the robot reports an error, resolve it before continuing. Read the current position with: Position The response format depends on the robot. X3 returns comma-separated XYZ coordinates; see Useful Commands for the model-specific formats. 6. Try a small movement ¶ Use absolute positioning to move the tool to specific coordinates. In this mode, X , Y , and Z are target positions in the robot’s current coordinate system, measured in millimeters. Send one line at a time and wait for Ok before the next line. Do not paste the entire sequence into the command field at once. After completing homing in step 5, select absolute positioning: G90 G90 selects the coordinate mode; it does not move the robot. Move to a starting position ¶ Choose one starting command for your robot. The examples use Z-360 for X3 and Z-750 from the XS G-code reference. For XS, check the workspace of your specific size and adjust Z before sending the command; Z-750 is not a common working height for every XS model. Confirm that the path to the starting position and the following 10 mm X movement are clear. If you have configured coordinate offsets, account for them when choosing the target. Delta X 3: move to the absolute position (0, 0, -360) : G01 X0 Y0 Z-360 F100 A1000 J10000 S0 E0 Delta X S: move to the absolute position (0, 0, -750) , using a Z value appropriate to your model: G01 X0 Y0 Z-750 F100 A1000 J10000 S0 E0 The starting command sets the feed rate to 100 mm/s, acceleration to 1000 mm/s², jerk to 10000 mm/s³, and start/end velocities to zero. These motion settings remain in effect for subsequent moves until changed; you only need to enter them once. Move along X and return ¶ For either robot, send: G01 X10 This moves to the absolute coordinate X = 10 mm , keeping Y and Z at the starting values. Sending G01 X10 again keeps the same target; it does not add another 10 mm. Return to X = 0 mm : G01 X0 The tool is now back at the starting position you selected above, with the same Y and Z. Absolute positioning remains active for the next movement commands. The screenshot shows a test using Z-650 for that setup, followed by G1 X10 and G1 X0 . Choose Z for your own robot as described above. G90 is not shown in the screenshot; send it before the movement commands to select absolute positioning. 7. Emergency stop and recovery ¶ Use Emergency:Stop when you need to interrupt robot movement because of an emergency. Enter the command in Termite and press Enter immediately; do not wait for the current movement’s Ok reply. Emergency:Stop The firmware replies Delta:Stop . Check that the robot has stopped, and stop sending movement commands. A serial emergency stop depends on the USB connection and firmware; use the physical emergency stop when immediate intervention is needed. Write these commands exactly as shown, with no space after the colon. Command Purpose Emergency:Stop Request an emergency stop and interrupt movement. Emergency:Resume Clear the software stop/pause condition so commands can run again. It does not restart the interrupted path from the stopping point. Emergency:Pause Request a pause. On the X3 and XS firmware covered by this guide, this also interrupts the active path; it is not a pause-and-continue function for that path. Emergency:Reset Restart the robot controller. Use it when a controller restart is required, then reconnect and home again. Recover after an emergency stop ¶ Identify and resolve the cause of the stop. Check the tool, workpiece, and robot’s position, then clear the working area. If the physical emergency-stop button was pressed, release it only after the cause has been resolved. A serial Resume command does not release the physical button. Confirm that no unwanted commands are waiting to run. The examples in this guide send one movement at a time. If you previously sent several movements ahead, follow Clear pending commands before resuming. Send: Emergency:Resume XS replies Delta:Resume ; X3 uses its configured completion reply, normally Ok . Resume allows commands to run again; it does not confirm the robot’s position or home it. Check that the homing path is clear, then send: G28 Wait for homing to finish before sending the next command. Re-homing is especially necessary if the stop interrupted homing, the motors were disabled, or the mechanism was moved. Restore absolute positioning and check the position, sending each line separately: G90 Position Review the next target and motion settings, then send a new movement command when ready. Do not assume the interrupted move reached its original target. Clear pending commands ¶ Emergency:Stop does not guarantee that queued commands have been cleared. Resume may allow pending commands to execute. On XS V5 , after the robot has stopped and before Resume, you can discard pending G-code commands with: Robot:QueueClear This clears waiting commands; it does not stop an active movement. It is not available in the X3 or XS V4 firmware covered here. For X3 or XS V4 , if you are unsure which commands remain queued, use the controller restart procedure below instead of resuming that queue. Pause and resume ¶ To request a pause, send: Emergency:Pause The firmware replies Delta:Pause . Before sending Emergency:Resume , review the robot state and any pending commands as described above. Send a new target for the next movement; Resume does not complete the interrupted path automatically. Restart the controller ¶ When a controller restart is required, first stop movement and stop sending commands, then send: Emergency:Reset The firmware replies Delta:Reset and restarts. The USB connection may disconnect; wait for the controller to restart, then reconnect Termite if needed. Send IsDelta to check communication, run G28 after checking the homing path, and select G90 before using the absolute movement examples again. Re-enter any settings that were not saved before the restart. 8. Disconnect normally ¶ Let the current movement finish, then click Termite’s connection status field to close the COM port, or close Termite. You do not need Emergency:Stop just to disconnect after normal operation. Closing the terminal does not stop a movement already executing. Troubleshooting ¶ Symptom What to check The robot does not appear in Device Manager Check power, the USB data cable, and the USB port. If Windows reports a driver issue, install the driver appropriate to the robot’s USB interface. Termite cannot open the COM port Select the correct port and close any other application using it. The sent command appears, but there is no robot reply Check that the port is connected, the baud rate is 115200 , and Append CR-LF is selected. Local echo is not a reply from the robot. The received text is unreadable Check the baud rate, data bits, parity, and stop bits against the settings above. IsDelta works but the robot will not move Check motor power and the stop state. If stopped, follow Emergency stop and recovery , then home with G28 and read any returned error. A movement command is rejected Check the command reference for the installed firmware, the current G90/G91 mode, and the robot’s workspace. For further commands, use the matching X3 reference , XS V4 reference , or XS V5 reference .
